title: Bank of Canada governor says rate hike to 2.5% was needed in face of persistent inflation

image.caption: Bank of Canada governor Tiff Macklem during a news conference in Ottawa on Wednesday. (Adrian Wyld/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Why now? Tiff Macklem asked what central bank aims to accomplish with rate hike

Bank of Canada governor Tiff Macklem, when asked what the central bank was trying to accomplish with its first rate hike since 2023, acknowledged the complexity of the global economic situation, particularly around increased energy prices. But he said the policy rate — even with the increase — is 'low enough that it's not restraining growth' but will help get inflation back to target 'more quickly.'

items: The Bank of Canada has raised its benchmark interest rate a quarter-point to 2.5 per cent.

The bank said the increase is needed to reduce the risk of higher energy prices fuelling broader inflation. Canada's annual inflation rate rose to 3.1 per cent in September, largely driven by surging energy prices due to the war in the Middle East.
The bank's governor Tiff Macklem had kept the interest rate at 2.25 for seven consecutive meetings. Today's hike marks the bank's first rate change in a year and the first rate hike since 2023.
Macklem faces a difficult balancing act: raising interest rates could help slow inflation, but could also weaken growth in an already struggling labour market.
The Bank of Canada's next rate decision is scheduled for Dec. 9.

October 28Takeaways from today's Bank of Canada rate hikeBank of Canada governor Tiff Macklem during a news conference in Ottawa on Wednesday. (Adrian Wyld/The Canadian Press)We're wrapping up our live coverage of the Bank of Canada's interest rate announcement. Here are some of the key takeaways from today's decision.The central bank raised its benchmark interest rate by a quarter-point to 2.5 per cent, marking its first change after seven consecutive holds and its first increase since July 2023.Governor Tiff Macklem said the hike was "needed to reduce the risk that elevated energy prices could spill over and become generalized inflation."As the war in the Middle East has kept oil prices high, the bank expects inflation to reach roughly 3.5 per cent by the end of 2026 and remain at or above three per cent for much of next year.The bank's outlook for economic growth has improved slightly, though, with the Canadian economy expected to grow two per cent next year. He also said the Canadian economy showed signs of resilience through the middle of 2026, growing 3.3 per cent in the second quarter.Still, Macklem noted that uncertainty surrounding U.S. tariffs and the conflict in the Middle East continues to weigh on the economy.Today's hike also means higher borrowing costs for Canadians, including prospective homebuyers. Deputy governor Carolyn Rogers said the housing market is already struggling, particularly in Ontario and British Columbia, and that the rate increase will add to those pressures.The bank hasn't ruled out more hikes, but Macklem stressed that future decisions will be made "one meeting at a time.""There could be a need to increase the policy rate further, but given uncertainties, Governing Council agreed to proceed carefully," the bank said.

Hike will weigh on variable mortgage holders: brokerAbby HughesHouses are pictured in Vancouver, B.C., on April 4, 2024. (Ben Nelms/CBC)Mortgage broker Marcus Tzaferis says today's rate decision might not do much to weigh on the housing market by keeping new buyers on the sidelines, because so many Canadians are already choosing not to buy.But it will weigh on mortgage holders.Those with variable rates will feel it the most. On a $500,000 mortgage, a rate hike of 25 basis points would add about $70 per month on average to a holder's monthly payments.While that might not seem like much, Tzaferis says Canadians are already struggling with the high cost of living, pointing to a rise in insolvencies as a sign consumers are having a tough time."To a consumer that's already stretched, these 25 basis point incremental increases are going to have an impact," Tzaferis said.For variable rate holders who are thinking about the impact that rising rates could have and want more predictability, Tzaferis says "now is the time" to try and lock in a fixed mortgage.And for those who will need to renegotiate a mortgage within the next year, Tzaferis says they have the option to lock in a fixed rate further in advance, "almost like an insurance policy for themselves," which could make sense for some.

Bank could've held off on raising rates, says economistAbby HughesPedro Antunes is the chief economist at Signal 49, an independent research firm. He says the bank could have held off longer before raising rates, but understands why the governing council would have wanted to guard against inflation. (CBC)Pedro Antunes, chief economist at independent research firm Signal 49, says he thinks the bank could have held off longer before raising rates.Looking at last month's inflation numbers, Antunes says inflation from oil still hasn't started spilling over into the cost of other prices yet. While the overall 3.1 inflation rate was high, core measures that strip out volatile items like oil were much lower and within the bank's target range."We haven't seen … a broader-based increase in prices, but I think that the bank has started to be concerned about what's coming down the road," Antunes told CBC News.And that concern is somewhat warranted, he said, especially after the bank didn't raise rates quickly in the face of high inflation post-COVID. The signal today is that the bank doesn't want a redo of that."I think the bank is concerned about this oil price shock playing a role here in the same way that it did in 2022. And you know, who can blame them? They're a little nervous about how that might play out."

Oil soars to US$103 per barrel, BoC sees no end in sight to war-linked inflationJeff LagerquistHere’s why you’re paying more for dieselCrude oil exports through the Strait of Hormuz are slowly recovering, so why is the price of diesel skyrocketing? The National's Eli Glasner breaks down what’s causing the increase, and why diesel prices likely won't drop anytime soon.Rising oil prices linked to war in the Middle East have been a persistent irritant for the Bank of Canada as it attempts to control inflation. That war could escalate in the coming weeks.U.S. officials have told several Gulf Arab countries to be prepared for a short, intense military campaign after the U.S. midterm elections on Nov. 3, the Wall Street Journal reported on Wednesday.The U.S. benchmark oil price soared nearly 3.5 per cent today, rising above $103 US per barrel. West Texas Intermediate crude is up nearly 70 per cent year-over-year. According to data from Kalibrate, Canadian pump prices for regular gasoline are up nearly 30 per cent on average versus this time last year. Diesel prices have soared over 70 per cent on an annualized basis.Here's what the Bank of Canada said about the situation earlier today:"The conflict in the Middle East is now in its eighth month, and there is no clear path to resolution. The combination of higher-for-longer energy prices, and increased pass-through, adds to the persistence of inflation in the projection."The prices of gasoline, diesel and heating oil are considerably higher than in July, and are expected to remain higher for longer. This is hitting consumers directly and raising business costs for production and transportation."

More hikes likely, but maybe not so soon: economistAbby HughesPeople pass the Bank of Montreal building in Toronto on Aug. 14, 2023. (Spencer Colby/The Canadian Press)Benjamin Reitzes, managing director at BMO Economics, says the central bank's messaging indicates further hikes will come — but maybe not soon.Despite the Bank of Canada warning that more rate hikes might be necessary, it also said it would proceed with caution. That "suggests a follow-up hike in December isn't a lock by any means," Reitzes said."There's likely more tightening to come, but the pace of further hikes is extremely uncertain and will be driven by the incoming data," he wrote in a note to investors.Reitzes says weak growth forecasted for the last few months of this year and continued trade uncertainty will be the things to watch — and that if momentum picks up there, that could trigger more increases.

Rate hike is bad news for businesses: CFIBAbby HughesSimon Gaudreault is the chief economist and vice-president of research at the Canadian Federation of Independent Business (CFIB). (Canadian Federation of Independent Business)Heading into today's decision, business owners across Canada were already in a tough spot. The trade war with the U.S. has been a significant weight and increased the cost of doing business, according to Simon Gaudreault, chief economist for the Canadian Federation of Independent Business (CFIB)."We're talking about entrepreneurs that have been entrepreneurs for 15, 20, 25 years or more, telling us that they've never seen such a challenging situation in terms of the operating costs," Gaudreault said.Today's rate hike could add to that pain for lots of businesses, he said. A rate hike would leave Canadian consumers with less cash in their pockets, which Gauldreaut says could hurt demand for business owners.Many business owners also have variable mortgages for business properties or hold other kinds of debt at floating rates, he said, meaning their costs will now be higher. It could also make it harder to take on new business investments, like upgrading equipment."The trade war hasn't brought that sort of certainty that you're looking for as an entrepreneur to invest. And so making the cost of capital even higher, even more expensive with the rate hike certainly won't help here."

Bank predict sluggish housing market, rate hike could dampen activityVerity StevensonBank of Canada's housing outlook 'pretty subdued' — but not just because of rates, official saysBank of Canada senior deputy governor Carolyn Rogers, speaking after the central bank hiked a key interest rate, said the organization's outlook for housing is 'pretty subdued' for a few reasons, including overall economic uncertainty.Deputy governor Carolyn Rogers acknowledged that the bank's interest rate hike will add to pressures on homebuyers."Certainly borrowing rates are currently weighing a bit on the housing market. An increase will add to that a bit on the margin," Rogers said.She said the bank expects Canada's housing market to remain sluggish over the next two years. Rogers said the bank's outlook for housing remains "pretty subdued," with growth forecast at about one per cent over the next two years."There's a number of things weighing on housing right now," Rogers said, pointing to broader uncertainty in the economy caused by inflation, energy costs and trade issues. "People don't tend to make big purchase decisions like housing in that kind of an environment."Rogers said the housing market is undergoing an adjustment, with particularly sharp slowdowns in British Columbia and Ontario, especially in Vancouver and Toronto.

Loonie wobbles post rate hike, expert sees 'weakness before the end of the year'Jeff LagerquistLoonies at the Royal Canadian Mint in Winnipeg on Nov. 14, 2023. (John Woods/The Canadian Press)The loonie is trading in a choppy fashion against U.S. dollar this morning, following the Bank of Canada's decision to hike its benchmark interest rate for the first time since July 2023.Canada's currency is currently worth $0.7124 US, according to Bloomberg data.Currency traders are struggling to reconcile the impact that higher borrowing costs could have on a still-weak Canadian economy, according to Karl Schamotta, chief market strategist at the payments company Corpay."Although we are bullish on the loonie over longer horizons, we remain convinced that markets are overpricing the Bank's tightening trajectory, and expect a bout of weakness before the end of the year as implied rate differentials widen against the currency again," he wrote in an online post on Wednesday.

Federal tax measures, major projects, higher oil exports expected to boost investmentVerity StevensonBank of Canada governor Tiff Macklem during today's news conference in Ottawa. (Adrian Wyld/The Canadian Press)Macklem was asked whether federal policies such as Carney's productivity mega deduction and the push to accelerate major projects improve the Canadian economic outlook. The governor said both those measures are predicted to help strengthen business investment in 2027, noting the economy is expected to grow by two per cent next year — a somewhat stronger outlook than the Bank of Canada had predicted in July. "There are some big projects through the Major Projects Office that will probably start to take shape next year. The mega deduction should support investment," Macklem said. The mega deduction, announced by Carney in September, allows companies to write off 100 per cent of the cost of eligible investments, such as machinery, from its taxable income in the year it becomes available for use, rather than deducting those costs gradually over several years. The bank predicts another factor will help the Canadian economy: Macklem said higher energy prices are also encouraging investment in Canada's oil and gas sector, with energy exports increasing.Still, Macklem cautioned that the bank has been relatively conservative in its assumptions about future investment."We've been disappointed in the past in investment in this country," he said. "We certainly think it'll be stronger. We'd like to be surprised it's even stronger than we've built in."

High oil costs out of Canada's control, so why hike?Abby HughesWhy now? Tiff Macklem asked what central bank aims to accomplish with rate hikeBank of Canada governor Tiff Macklem, when asked what the central bank was trying to accomplish with its first rate hike since 2023, acknowledged the complexity of the global economic situation, particularly around increased energy prices. But he said the policy rate — even with the increase — is 'low enough that it's not restraining growth' but will help get inflation back to target 'more quickly.'Because inflation is being driven by high oil prices — which are out of Canada's control — a reporter asked Macklem what he hoped to achieve by raising interest rates.Macklem said the goal with the rate hike is to contain inflation and prevent high energy costs from upping the cost of other products Canadians would buy at stores.As oil prices have been elevated for months on end with no end in sight, Macklem said businesses have indicated in the bank's surveys that they intend to pass on some of those energy costs to consumers. "Canadians are already paying for more at the pump. And we can't … change that," Macklem said. But what would be worse is if Canadians had to "pay for it twice" because of that passthrough.He says the hike is low enough that it shouldn't hamper growth too much but should also help get inflation back to its target range more quickly.
